t.7.67.1: Having heard those words of Rāma, whose deeds were unwearied, he, in that state, with his head bowed down, spoke these words.
t.7.67.2: I was born from a śūdra womb and have undertaken fierce austerity. O Rāma of great renown, I seek godhood while still in this very body.
t.7.67.3: I do not speak falsely, O king; it is out of a desire to conquer the world of the gods. Know me to be a Śūdra, O Kākutstha, Śambūka by name.
t.7.67.4: Even as that Śūdra was still speaking, Rāghava drew from its sheath a spotless sword of brilliant radiance and cut off his head.
t.7.67.5: At that very moment, that boy was united with life once more.
t.7.67.6: Then lotus-eyed Rāma went to the hermitage of Agastya, and bowing to him with all humility, he rejoiced, filled with happiness.
t.7.67.7: Having saluted the great-souled one, who seemed to blaze with splendor, and having received the highest hospitality, the lord of men sat down.
t.7.67.8: To him spoke the pot-born one, of great splendour and great austerity: "Welcome to you, best of men! By good fortune you have arrived, Rāghava."
t.7.67.9: O Rāma, you are highly esteemed by me for your many excellent virtues; you are a guest worthy of honour, and, O king, you dwell in my heart.
t.7.67.10: For the gods speak of you, who have come here, as the slayer of the Śūdra; and through righteousness the brāhmaṇa's son has been restored to life by you.
t.7.67.11: Stay here tonight in my presence, O Rāghava; at daybreak you shall go to your own city by the Puṣpaka.
t.7.67.12: And this divine ornament, gentle one, fashioned by Viśvakarman, blazing with its own splendour and with a divine form, accept it, Kākutstha; do what is dear to me, Rāghava.
t.7.67.13: For the giving again of what has once been given is said to bear very great fruit. Therefore I shall give it according to the rites; accept it, O bull among men.
t.7.67.14: Rāma accepted from that great-souled sage that divine and wondrous ornament, which shone like the blazing sun.
t.7.67.15: Rāma, reaching out, accepted that excellent ornament and then began to ask about the origin of that divine object.
t.7.67.16: O Brahmin, this is most wondrous and supreme, endowed with a splendid form. How was it obtained by you, revered one? From where, or by whom, was it brought?
t.7.67.17: Out of curiosity, O brahmin of great renown, I ask you this, for you are indeed the supreme treasury of many wonders.
t.7.67.18: When Kākutstha spoke thus, the sage then said these words: "Listen, Rāma, to what happened long ago, in the Tretā age now gone by."
